option.label: Sessile FIRST glume: upper margins winged
option.detail: Locate the first outer glume on a stalkless spikelet; Angleton’s upper margins may be slightly winged. Not a winged flowering rachis.

option_additions.subgroup: First glume: sessile versus stalked spikelet

option.label: Sessile FIRST glume: broad, blunt apex
option.detail: Inspect the apex of the first glume of the sessile spikelet. Gould describes it as typically broad and obtuse; do not substitute the lemma apex.

option_additions.subgroup: First glume: sessile versus stalked spikelet

option.label: Sessile FIRST glume: papilla-based marginal/basal hairs
option.detail: Trace hairs to the first glume’s margins and base. These papilla-based glume hairs are separate from blade hairs and KR stiff hairs on the lower glume back.

option_additions.subgroup: First glume: sessile versus stalked spikelet

option.label: Flowering rachis / pedicels stiff-hairy
option.detail: Angleton’s branch rachis and pedicels are hispid, sometimes villous. Do not relabel ordinary stiff hairs as a medial groove.

option.label: Main flowering axis / branch bases hairy
option.detail: Inspect the MAIN inflorescence axis and the bases of its branches. Gould contrasts Angleton’s pubescence here with Kleberg’s hairlessness.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect young and older culm nodes
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Angleton nodes begin densely bearded but frequently become hairless with age. Blades may be hairless or sparsely stiff-hairy with papilla bases; sheaths are hairless.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: KR also has age-related node hair loss; do not exclude either on an old hairless node.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published exact-taxon evidence, with age/organ/source scope; no specimen or county-occurrence certification.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, printed p.559, Dichanthium aristatum

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Locate flowering-axis pubescence and sessile first-glume hairs
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould describes Angleton’s main axis/branch bases as pubescent, and rachis/pedicels hispid, sometimes villous. Its sessile first glume has a typically broad blunt tip, slightly winged upper margins and often papilla-based hairs at margins/base.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Kleberg’s axis/branch bases are hairless; these features are separate from KR grooves and first-glume lower-back hairs.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published exact-taxon evidence, with age/organ/source scope; no specimen or county-occurrence certification.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, printed p.559, Dichanthium aristatum

learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould gives a weakly twice-geniculate, twisted brownish awn 15–25 mm. Inflorescence has 3–5(2–8) spicate branches mostly 4–7 cm long; sessile spikelets 4–5 mm.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Retain source ranges and organ identity. No Angleton groove absence or pedicelled awnlessness is inferred from the neighboring Kleberg treatment.

learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Do not call every Kleberg spikelet awned or every sessile one awnless from a single basal pair.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Compare the two books without transferring Angleton measurements

option.label: Flowering branches / pedicels lack medial groove
option.detail: Diggs explicitly describes Kleberg pedicels and inflorescence branches without a groove or membranous area. Confirm the actual organ; a ridge or hair line is not a groove.

option.label: LOWEST spikelet pairs usually awnless
option.detail: Diggs describes Kleberg’s lowest branch pairs as usually awnless and not seed-producing. This does not make its upper fertile spikelets awnless.

option.label: Culm node with long white hair ring
option.detail: Diggs describes a conspicuous ring of long white hairs at Kleberg culm nodes. These are not hairs at a flowering rachis node or the ligule.
